questions.stem: Do arteries always carry oxygenated blood?

options.text: Yes — arteries always carry oxygenated blood
No — arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs
Yes — but only in mammals
No — arteries always carry deoxygenated blood

questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart — this is their definition, not the type of blood they carry. Most arteries carry oxygenated blood, but the pulmonary artery is the exception — it carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Similarly, the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood to the heart.

questions.stem: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the right ventricle?

options.text: Because the left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs only
Because the left ventricle pumps blood to the entire body (systemic circulation), requiring higher pressure
Because the right ventricle is stronger
There is no difference in wall thickness

questions.explanation: The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall because it needs to generate much higher pressure to pump blood through the entire body (systemic circulation). The right ventricle only pumps blood the short distance to the lungs (pulmonary circulation), so it needs less pressure and has a thinner wall.

questions.stem: What is the role of valves in the heart and veins?

options.text: To increase blood pressure
To prevent the backflow of blood, ensuring it flows in one direction only
To filter blood as it passes through
To produce red blood cells

questions.explanation: Valves prevent the backflow of blood, ensuring it flows in one direction. In the heart, the tricuspid and bicuspid (mitral) valves prevent backflow from ventricles to atria, while the semilunar valves prevent backflow from arteries to ventricles. Valves in veins help blood flow back to the heart against gravity.

questions.stem: What is a double circulatory system?

options.text: A system where blood passes through the heart once per circuit
A system where blood passes through the heart twice per complete circuit — once for the pulmonary circulation and once for the systemic circulation
A system with two hearts
A system where blood flows in both directions through the same vessel

questions.explanation: In a double circulatory system, blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit: first through the pulmonary circuit (heart → lungs → heart, for gas exchange) and then through the systemic circuit (heart → body → heart, to deliver oxygen and nutrients). This maintains higher blood pressure for efficient delivery.

questions.stem: Why do red blood cells have no nucleus?

options.text: Because they are not real cells
To provide more space for haemoglobin, allowing them to carry more oxygen
Because the nucleus is too heavy for blood cells
Because all blood cells lack a nucleus

questions.explanation: Mature red blood cells lose their nucleus during development to make more space for haemoglobin — the protein that binds to and carries oxygen. They also have a biconcave disc shape, which increases the surface area to volume ratio for more efficient gas exchange. White blood cells DO have a nucleus.

options.text: The main arteries leaving the heart
The blood vessels that supply the heart muscle itself with oxygenated blood and nutrients
The arteries that carry blood to the lungs
The veins that return blood to the heart

questions.explanation: The coronary arteries branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle (myocardium) with oxygenated blood and glucose for respiration. The heart muscle needs its own blood supply because it contracts continuously. If coronary arteries become blocked (coronary heart disease), the heart muscle is starved of oxygen, leading to a heart attack.

questions.stem: Why do capillaries have walls that are only one cell thick?

options.text: Because they need to withstand high blood pressure
To provide a short diffusion distance for efficient exchange of substances (oxygen, glucose, CO₂) between blood and tissues
To prevent blood from leaking out
Because they are too small for thicker walls

questions.explanation: Capillary walls are only one cell (endothelium) thick to minimise the diffusion distance between blood and surrounding tissues. This allows rapid and efficient exchange of substances: oxygen and glucose diffuse from blood to tissues, while CO₂ and waste diffuse from tissues to blood. Capillaries also have a narrow lumen and slow blood flow to maximise exchange time.

questions.stem: What are the four main components of blood?

options.text: Water, salt, glucose, oxygen
Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets
Haemoglobin, antibodies, urea, hormones
Arteries, veins, capillaries, heart

questions.explanation: Blood has four main components: plasma (the liquid part, carrying dissolved substances like glucose, urea, hormones, and CO₂), red blood cells (carry oxygen using haemoglobin), white blood cells (immune defence — phagocytes and lymphocytes), and platelets (cell fragments involved in blood clotting).

options.text: A condition where veins become blocked
The build-up of fatty deposits (plaques) inside artery walls, narrowing the lumen and restricting blood flow
An infection of the heart muscle
A condition where blood cannot clot

questions.explanation: Atherosclerosis is the build-up of fatty deposits (atheroma/plaques) within the walls of arteries. This narrows the lumen, restricts blood flow, and increases blood pressure. If a coronary artery is affected, it can lead to coronary heart disease and potentially a heart attack. Risk factors include high-fat diet, smoking, lack of exercise, and genetic predisposition.

questions.stem: How do arteries, veins, and capillaries differ in structure?

options.text: They all have the same structure
Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls and a narrow lumen; veins have thinner walls, a wider lumen, and valves; capillaries have walls one cell thick
Veins have the thickest walls; arteries have the thinnest
Only capillaries have a lumen; arteries and veins do not

questions.explanation: Arteries have thick walls with muscle and elastic tissue (to withstand and maintain high pressure) and a narrow lumen. Veins have thinner walls, a wider lumen (lower pressure), and valves to prevent backflow. Capillaries have walls only one cell thick and a very narrow lumen (just wide enough for one red blood cell) for efficient diffusion.
